title: Why this course exists: verification is the job
body:
- LLMs write analytics code faster than you ever will. What they don't do is guarantee the number is right.
- Agent output is fluent, plausible, and wrong in ways only a capable reader catches — like proofreading a translation into a language you can't read.
- The defensible skills: verification, specification, code literacy, and accountability for the number.
- You graduate able to sign the number: to say "this figure is right, and here is why," with your name on it.
managerial_phrasing: The agent produces the draft; you produce the guarantee. The person who can certify the number is the one the firm can't replace.
common_mistake: Treating the course as 'learn to code.' It's 'learn to read and audit code' — writing is the agent's job; catching what's wrong is yours.

title: The analytics cycle: Ask, Acquire, Analyze, Answer
body:
- Every real analysis runs the same four stages: Ask (frame a question the data can answer), Acquire (get and clean the data), Analyze (compute and model), Answer (a memo a decision-maker can act on).
- The course runs the cycle twice: cycle 1 guided on Eastville housing (inference), cycle 2 open on loan default (prediction), with your own team question.
- Topics exist only because a stage demands them. If you're lost, locate yourself in the cycle first.
managerial_phrasing: Before touching data, name where you are: what's the question, what data answers it, what did we compute, what do we tell the decision-maker.
common_mistake: Jumping to Analyze with an unframed question — the most expensive errors are made before any code runs.

title: Two tiers: Understand vs Recipe 🔧
body:
- Understand tier: few things, examinable, reinforced with multiple business examples. You must be able to read, predict, and explain this code.
- Recipe tier (🔧): use it, trust it, don't dissect it. Examples: the read_csv encoding argument, the smf.ols incantation, sklearn's fit/predict.
- You are never expected to understand every character of a recipe cell. Knowing which tier a line belongs to is itself a skill.
managerial_phrasing: Distinguish what you must be able to defend from what you correctly use as a trusted tool — and say which is which.
common_mistake: Two symmetric failures: panicking over recipe syntax you were never meant to internalize, or treating Understand-tier material as copy-paste boilerplate.

title: AI norms are per-beat: forbidden, assistant, adversary, auditee
body:
- Forbidden: screens down, your own reading (e.g., Read & Predict beats, exams).
- Assistant: allowed with disclosure plus one checking sentence stating how you verified the output.
- Adversary: the AI produces an analysis you must attack.
- Auditee: the AI's work is the object under audit.
- Disclosure is never penalized. Undisclosed use is the violation, not use.
managerial_phrasing: State the tool's role before using it: was the AI drafting for me, checking me, or being checked by me?
common_mistake: Assuming one blanket rule for the whole course. The mode changes beat by beat, and the disclosure-plus-check sentence is mandatory in assistant mode.

title: Signing the number
body:
- The end state of every analysis: which figures would you put your name on, with what caveat, and which would you refuse?
- Signing requires tracing each flaw's blast radius: a duplicate-row problem upstream infects every average downstream.
- Three honest verdicts exist: sign it · sign it with a stated caveat · don't sign it. "Looks right" is not a verdict.
managerial_phrasing: For each headline number: I stand behind this / I stand behind this given X / I cannot certify this — one sentence each.
common_mistake: Flagging every number to be safe. False alarms cost credibility just as missed flaws do; the exams penalize both.

title: Anatomy of an answerable question
body:
A question the data can answer has three properties:
- A defined outcome: the thing measured is stated precisely enough that two people would compute the same number.
- Matching grain: the level of the rows (one row = one house, one loan) matches the level of the question.
- An attached decision: someone will do something differently depending on the answer.
Questions failing these die at Ask or Acquire — before any analysis could save them.
managerial_phrasing: State the outcome, the unit, and the decision in one sentence: 'For [decision], we need [measure] per [unit].'
common_mistake: Starting from the dataset ('what can we do with these columns?') instead of the decision — dataset-first drift produces answers nobody asked for.

title: The kill test
body:
- Before investing in a question, try to kill it: What outcome exactly? At what grain? Could any dataset answer it? Would the answer change a decision?
- A question that survives the kill test is worth acquiring data for; one that dies saved you weeks.
- Introduced stripped-down in cycle 1; the full version governs your cycle-2 brief.
managerial_phrasing: Attack your own question before your data does: if we had a perfect dataset, what number would settle this — and can we define that number?
common_mistake: Treating the kill test as a formality to pass rather than an honest attempt to break the question — soft attacks let doomed questions through.

title: Disease: undefined outcome
body:
- The question names no measurable outcome, or one so vague that different analysts would compute different numbers ('is the market healthy?', 'which loans are good?').
- Everything downstream inherits the ambiguity: the analysis computes something, and the memo pretends it was the thing asked.
- Headline trap of the Framing topic. Cure: define the outcome as a column you could point to, or a formula over columns.
managerial_phrasing: Before we pull data: what exact number, computed how, on what unit, would answer this?
common_mistake: Believing the outcome is 'obvious.' If it isn't written as something computable, two teammates are silently answering different questions.

title: Disease: dataset-first drift
body:
- The team starts from available data and drifts toward whatever question the columns make easy, rather than the question the decision needs.
- Symptom: the brief's question mutates to match the dataset between scoping and delivery, without anyone deciding that.
- Secondary trap of the Framing topic.
managerial_phrasing: Are we answering the question we were asked, or the question this file happens to make convenient?
common_mistake: Rationalizing drift as pragmatism. Adapting to data constraints is fine only when the change is named, justified, and accepted by the decision-maker.

title: Disease: wrong grain
body:
- The rows are at the wrong level for the question: school-level averages can't answer a listing-level question; borrower-level data can't answer a payment-level question.
- The Eastville version is stark: two school zones means a 'school averages' one-pager has two rows — self-evidently unable to price one house.
- Aggregated data destroys within-group variation; no later step recovers it. Cure: restate the question's unit, then check what one row represents.
managerial_phrasing: One row of this table is a ___. Our question is about a ___. If those don't match, this data can't answer it.
common_mistake: Assuming averages of averages are harmless. Group-level summaries silently weight and blur exactly the differences the question is about.

title: Variables, assignment, and types
body:
- A variable is a labeled value: revenue = 48_500_000. Assignment (=) stores; it doesn't compare.
- Types matter because operations depend on them: the number 48500000 can grow by 4%; the text "48.5M" cannot.
- The course's founding example: a price stored as "$249,310" won't average — the dollar sign makes it text. Types are why the cleaning chain exists.
- Text in quotes is a string; numbers without quotes compute. A date stored as text sorts alphabetically, not chronologically.
managerial_phrasing: When a computation refuses to run or gives nonsense, ask first: is this column stored as text or as a number?
common_mistake: Reading '$249,310' as a number because it looks like one. Formatting characters make it text, and every average built on it fails or lies.

title: Function call vs method call
body:
- Function call: name(thing) — pd.read_csv('file.csv'). The tool comes first, the object goes inside.
- Method call: thing.action() — df['price'].mean(). The object comes first; the dot means 'do this to it.'
- Chains read left to right: df['price'].str.replace('$','').astype(float) is three actions applied in sequence.
managerial_phrasing: Read the dot as 'then': take the column, then strip the symbol, then convert to number.
common_mistake: Reading a method chain right to left, or treating the chain as one magic word instead of a sequence of separate, checkable steps.

title: Booleans, comparisons, and filtering with masks
body:
- A comparison (==, >=, >) produces True or False — a value you can store: is_profitable = margin > 0.
- A boolean mask asks the comparison of every row at once: df['beds'] >= 4 is a column of True/False.
- df[mask] keeps only the True rows. Two conditions combine with & and parentheses: df[(df['school']=='Apple Valley') & (df['beds']>=4)].
- Excel anchor: this is Filter, written down — which makes it auditable and repeatable.
managerial_phrasing: Filtering is asking a true/false question of every row and keeping the yeses.
common_mistake: Using = (assignment) where == (comparison) is meant, and forgetting parentheses around each condition when combining with &.

title: Missing values: the isna/dropna decision
body:
- .isna() / .notna() find the holes; .dropna() removes rows containing them.
- Dropping is a decision, not hygiene: you must know how many rows leave and whether they differ systematically from the rows that stay.
- The protocol: count missing per column → ask why they're missing → then choose drop, fill, or keep-and-flag — and write the choice down.
- In Eastville, house 8's age is genuinely blank: your first real missing-data decision.
managerial_phrasing: Before removing incomplete rows: how many are we losing, and are they a random few or a biased slice?
common_mistake: Calling dropna() reflexively. If missingness is concentrated (older homes, defaulters), dropping quietly rewrites the population you're studying.

title: Lists and dictionaries
body:
- A list is ordered items in brackets: quarters = ["Q1","Q2","Q3","Q4"]. Grows with .extend().
- A dictionary is labeled values in braces: {"KO": 120, "MSFT": 40} — labels beat positions. Access by key: portfolio["KO"].
- Why you care: APIs answer in dictionaries (one dict per record), and pd.DataFrame(records) turns a list of dicts into a table.
- One customer record from any CRM export is a dict: {"name": ..., "segment": ..., "ltv": ...}.
managerial_phrasing: A dict is one record with named fields; a list of dicts is a table waiting to happen.
common_mistake: Confusing brackets and braces, or trying to grab a dict value by position instead of by its key.

title: The for loop
body:
- for item in collection: repeats the indented block once per item — the same work applied to each element.
- The founding use: the API answers in pages; the loop fetches every page and .extend()s one list until the data is complete.
- Other canonical uses: run the same market summary for three cities; check every column for missing values (the audit loop).
- The loop returns at s10 (for amenity in [...]) and comes full circle at s21 (for model in models:) — same construct, bigger objects.
managerial_phrasing: A loop is 'do this same thing for each of these' — if you'd copy-paste a block three times, a loop is the honest version.
common_mistake: Forgetting that only the indented lines repeat, and accumulating results by overwriting a variable instead of extending a list.

title: f-strings: numbers into sentences
body:
- f"Typical Eastville home: ${median:,.0f}" injects a computed value into a sentence; the :,.0f formats with commas, no decimals.
- Every number needs a caption — a number without a sentence is not yet an answer.
- Inside a loop, f-strings caption at scale: f"{school}: {n} homes, avg ${avg:,.0f}".
- Honest captions label trust level too: f"Basement premium: ${prem:,.0f} (naive)".
managerial_phrasing: Numbers don't speak; captions do. The f-string is where a computation becomes a claim.
common_mistake: Hard-coding the number into the sentence — when the data changes, the prose silently lies.

title: if — the sanity check
body:
- if condition: runs its block only when the condition is True.
- Its course role is the guard: if len(df) != 108: print("⚠ row count off") after every load; if df['price'].min() <= 0: print("⚠ impossible price").
- Self-checking code is the course thesis in one line: your notebook should catch its own problems before you present them.
- Also drives caption logic: if mean > median: skew_note = "right-skewed".
managerial_phrasing: Every load and every key number gets a guard: a line of code that shouts if reality disagrees with expectation.
common_mistake: Writing guards after something already broke. The guard's value is catching the problem you didn't expect — install them at load time, every time.

title: Functions: read and modify, don't compose
body:
- def name(parameter): packages a block; return hands back the result. You edit functions here — you are not asked to write them cold.
- The founding case: compare(amenity) runs the same naive-vs-adjusted analysis for any amenity — the function is the package, the loop over amenities is the repetition.
- Reuse pattern: def summarize(column): packages the s6 descriptive block; def load_eastville(): packages the whole cleaning pipeline as one call.
- If you can read a function well enough to change one thing safely, you can audit one.
managerial_phrasing: A function is analysis you trust enough to reuse: name it, feed it a parameter, get the standard output.
common_mistake: Editing inside a function without checking what the parameter controls — change the input, not scattered hard-coded values.

title: 🔧 Recipe: load and clean a CSV
body:
The standard opening block — use it, trust it:
- pd.read_csv('file.csv', encoding=...) → then .head(), .info(), .dtypes to see what arrived.
- Price-as-text fix: df['price'] = df['price'].str.replace('$','').str.replace(',','').astype(float).
- Duplicates: df.duplicated() to count, df.drop_duplicates(subset=['house']) to fix — subset names the column that defines 'same record.'
- Save the cleaned file with .to_csv(); downstream work reads the clean file, never re-cleans.
By s6 you can explain each piece; on day one you only need to run it and check the result.
managerial_phrasing: Loading isn't done until you've verified what arrived: row count, column types, and whether any 'number' is secretly text.
common_mistake: Running the chain without the checks — the recipe's value is the verification after it, not the incantation itself.

title: Out of scope: Python we deliberately cut
body:
Cut and stays cut: while loops · try/except · .loc/.iloc and the index concept · list comprehensions · OOP/classes.
- Masks plus column selection cover everything this course does; the cut items add power you don't need at reading-fluency cost you can't afford.
- If an AI hands you code using these, that's normal — you can ask it to rewrite with course constructs, or flag the cell as recipe-tier.
- Python is complete by session 10. Cycle 2 adds zero new core Python; everything after is fluency.
managerial_phrasing: We read a small dialect fluently rather than a large one badly — anything outside it gets translated in or trusted as a recipe.
common_mistake: Believing you're behind because online examples use comprehensions or .loc. Different dialect, not deeper knowledge.

title: APIs, JSON, and the pagination problem
body:
- An API answers requests with structured records — dictionaries — usually in pages (e.g., 25 records per response), not all at once.
- One page looks complete. It isn't: the loop that requests every page and extends one list is what makes the pull complete.
- The check is a count you can defend: does the assembled table's row count match what the source says exists?
- pd.DataFrame(records) turns the accumulated list of dicts into a table. This is the 'beyond Excel' move — no spreadsheet does this.
managerial_phrasing: When data comes from a feed, completeness is our job: we prove we got everything, not assume the first response was all of it.
common_mistake: Partial pull: analyzing page 1 as if it were the population. The numbers compute fine — on a quarter of reality.

title: SQL as a third syntax for known ideas
body:
- SELECT/WHERE/GROUP BY/ORDER BY/JOIN are pandas ideas in warehouse clothing: WHERE is a mask, GROUP BY is groupby, JOIN is merge.
- New syntax, zero new concepts — every clause sits beside its pandas twin. pd.read_sql brings results back to familiar ground.
- SQL matters because real data lives in warehouses; the analyst who can read the query can audit what was pulled.
- Join danger transfers too: a join can multiply rows (fan-out) in SQL exactly as merge can in pandas.
managerial_phrasing: Same filter-group-summarize logic you know — third language. What matters is checking the row count after every join.
common_mistake: Treating SQL as a new subject. It's translation; the diseases (fan-out, NULLs) transfer with the concepts.

title: 🔧 LLM as extractor — with a checking step
body:
- An LLM can turn unstructured text (documents, descriptions) into columns — a black-box recipe cell with one non-negotiable attachment: the checking step.
- The check: sample the extractions against the source text and count agreement; an extractor you haven't spot-checked is a rumor generator.
- Fluency is the hazard: extracted values arrive formatted and confident whether or not they're right.
managerial_phrasing: The model read the documents and filled the table; we verified a sample by hand before trusting any column.
common_mistake: Confident misextraction: shipping LLM-extracted columns unchecked because they look clean. Clean-looking is what wrong looks like now.

title: Disease: type confusion
body:
- Numbers stored as text ("$249,310", "48.5M", dates as strings) load without error and then fail or lie under arithmetic and sorting.
- Symptom: .info() shows 'object' where you expected a number; .mean() errors or a sort orders alphabetically.
- Headline trap of the Loading topic. Cure: check dtypes at load; apply the cleaning chain; re-verify with a computed statistic you can eyeball.
managerial_phrasing: Is every column that should be a number actually a number? Formatted exports routinely aren't.
common_mistake: Trusting appearance over dtype. A column can display as prices and be text — the failure surfaces two steps later, blamed on the wrong cell.

title: Disease: silent row loss
body:
- Rows disappear without announcement — a dropna(), a filter, a join — and the analysis proceeds on a quietly different population.
- The catastrophic form (s19): dropna() on the loan file deletes essentially every defaulter, because a rate field is blank for 99.5% of defaulters and 0% of payers. Default rate 'improves' from 24.6% to zero.
- Headline trap of Cleaning. Cure: row-count guards before and after every dropping operation, plus a check of who left.
managerial_phrasing: Between raw and analyzed, how many rows did we lose, at which step, and do the lost rows differ from the kept ones?
common_mistake: Believing missingness is random. When the blanks correlate with the outcome, dropping them doesn't clean the data — it deletes the phenomenon.

title: Disease: duplicate rows
body:
- The same record appears more than once (relisted homes, re-submitted loans), silently inflating counts and shifting averages toward the duplicated cases.
- Eastville's teaching file arrives with 111 rows for 108 homes — the first mystery you solve.
- Secondary trap of Cleaning (headline: silent row loss). Cure: define what makes a record unique, count duplicated() on that key, drop_duplicates(subset=...), and re-verify n.
managerial_phrasing: Is one row one real thing? If the same house can appear twice, every average is quietly wrong.
common_mistake: Deduplicating on the entire row when the ID column defines uniqueness — twins on every field except a timestamp survive the cleanse.

title: Disease: fan-out duplication (the join face)
body:
- Joining tables at different grains multiplies rows: loans joined to payments puts one loan on many rows; Eastville's warehouse join turns 8,400 rows into 9,100.
- Every downstream aggregate then overweights the multiplied records — same arithmetic as duplicate rows, manufactured by the join.
- Headline trap of the Joins topic, in both pandas merge and SQL JOIN. Cure: know each table's grain before joining; compare row counts before and after; if counts grew, say why or fix it.
managerial_phrasing: After every join: did the row count change, and does the result's grain still match the question's grain?
common_mistake: Assuming a join only adds columns. Joins can add rows — and a grown table silently changes what every average means.

title: Disease: NULL surprise
body:
- In SQL, NULLs vanish from comparisons and aggregates without notice: WHERE amount > 0 drops NULL rows silently; AVG ignores them; COUNT(col) ≠ COUNT(*).
- The query runs clean and the answer is computed on an unannounced subset.
- Headline trap of the SQL topic; secondary: a biased slice at source (the warehouse view was already filtered before you arrived).
- Cure: count NULLs per column first; know whether each aggregate includes or excludes them; ask what filter created the view you were handed.
managerial_phrasing: Which rows does this query silently ignore, and was the table already someone else's filtered opinion before we queried it?
common_mistake: Assuming SQL treats missing like pandas does. NULL logic is its own regime, and 'the query ran' proves nothing about completeness.

title: Disease: partial pull
body:
- Acquisition stops early — one page of a paginated API, a truncated export, a capped query — and the fragment is analyzed as the whole.
- Everything downstream computes correctly on incomplete reality; no error message will ever fire.
- Headline trap of Acquisition; secondary: structure drift (the source changes format mid-pull and later records parse wrong).
- Cure: an expected-count check against the source, plus the completion loop, plus a guard: if len(df) != expected: warn.
managerial_phrasing: How do we know we have all of it? 'The download finished' and 'the data is complete' are different claims.
common_mistake: Trusting a clean-looking first page. Completeness is proven with a count, never assumed from tidiness.

title: Disease: confident misextraction
body:
- An LLM extractor returns wrong values with perfect formatting: plausible rents, invented dates, the right schema around wrong facts.
- Unlike a crashed parser, nothing signals failure — the errors are only visible against the source text.
- Headline trap of the LLM topic. Cure: hand-verify a random sample against the source; report the agreement rate with the extraction; never trust a column you haven't sampled.
managerial_phrasing: Machine-extracted columns come with an error rate; we measured ours on a sample before using the data.
common_mistake: Equating well-formatted with correct. Fluent structure is the LLM's default even when the content is fabricated.

title: Disease: found-data bias
body:
- A convenient found dataset embeds its collection process: who's in it, who's missing, and what rule generated the outcome.
- The course exhibit: the rejected loan_approval file — 4,269 rows, demographic splits suspiciously near 50/50, and approval driven almost entirely by one rule (cibil_score > 550 → ~95% approval). It's synthetic, and it teaches whatever its generator assumed.
- Secondary trap of the LLM/found-data topic. Cure: interrogate provenance before columns — who collected this, how, and what can it not contain?
managerial_phrasing: Before using found data: where did it come from, who is missing from it, and could its patterns be the collector's rules rather than the world's?
common_mistake: Auditing only the columns. A pristine file can be unusable because the collection process, not the values, carries the bias.

title: Describing one variable: center, spread, shape
body:
- .describe(), .quantile(), .sort_values(), and a histogram give center, spread, and shape; Excel anchor: the descriptive-stats ribbon and sorting.
- Center is a choice: Eastville's mean price is $341,395, its median $331,715 — the gap is the outliers' signature (skew 1.25, a $675K home in a $197K–$675K range).
- Report the median when the distribution is skewed and say so; report both when the audience needs the total (means scale to totals; medians don't).
managerial_phrasing: Typical Eastville home: about $332K (median); the mean runs $10K higher because a few large homes pull it up.
common_mistake: Defaulting to the mean because it's familiar. Under skew the mean describes the outliers' gravity, not the typical case.

title: Comparing groups: groupby and aggregation
body:
- df.groupby('school')['price'].mean() computes one summary per group — the Pivot Table, written down. .agg() takes several summaries at once.
- Always carry the group sizes: an average without its n is a rumor. Eastville's 3-car-garage homes average $496K — on eight homes.
- The naive basement comparison lives here: basement homes (n=91) average $65,160 more than the rest (n=17). True, and not yet meaningful.
managerial_phrasing: Group A runs $X above group B — based on n of each — and the groups may differ in other ways we haven't controlled.
common_mistake: Reading a group gap as the feature's worth. A raw gap is a fact about the groups, not a price for the feature.

title: Rates and shares: value_counts and crosstab
body:
- value_counts() counts categories; normalize=True turns counts into shares — the difference between '91 homes have basements' and '84% of homes do.'
- crosstab / pivot_table cross two categoricals: basement rate by school zone (91% in Apple Valley vs 74% in Plum Ridge) is how composition differences surface.
- These composition tables are the confound-hunting instrument: they show that groups differ in several ways at once.
managerial_phrasing: Show the mix, not just the counts: what share of each group has the feature, and does that mix differ across segments?
common_mistake: Comparing raw counts across groups of different sizes — shares compare; counts mislead.

title: Correlation and the scatter plot
body:
- .corr() puts a number (−1 to 1) on linear association; the scatter shows what the number summarizes — and what it hides.
- Excel anchor: CORREL and the scatter chart.
- Correlation is symmetric and causeless: sqft and price move together; the number doesn't say which drives which, or whether a third thing drives both.
managerial_phrasing: These two move together (r = X); whether one causes the other is a separate question we haven't answered.
common_mistake: Reading r as importance or causation. A strong correlation is a lead, not a verdict — and a curved pattern can hide behind a modest r.

title: Disease: mean under skew
body:
- 'Typical' is reported as the mean while the printed distribution is visibly right-skewed — the number describes the tail's pull, not the common case.
- Eastville is the modest version (mean exceeds median by ~$10K); incomes and housing markets supply drastic ones.
- Headline trap of one-variable description. Cure: histogram first, mean-vs-median check, and a caption naming which center you chose and why.
managerial_phrasing: Which 'typical' are we reporting — the average dollar or the middle case — and would the audience decide differently under the other one?
common_mistake: Assuming mean and median tell one story. Under skew they diverge, and the mean flatters whichever tail is long.

title: Disease: small-group extremes
body:
- The most extreme group averages are the smallest groups: Eastville's 3-car homes average $496,349 on n=8; 1-car homes $258,335 on n=4.
- Small samples wander far from truth by luck alone, so a ranked table of group means is often a ranked table of sample sizes in disguise.
- Headline trap of Aggregation. Cure: print n beside every group mean; refuse to headline any group below a sanity threshold; say 'based on 8 homes' out loud.
managerial_phrasing: The extreme cells of any breakdown are usually the thin ones — check the n before believing the ranking.
common_mistake: Headlining the best or worst segment without its sample size. The 'top segment' on n=4 is noise wearing a crown.

title: Disease: the confounded gap
body:
- A raw group gap is narrated as the feature's value while the groups differ in other ways: Eastville's basement homes carry more beds (3.7 vs 3.3), more baths (2.7 vs 2.4), and sit disproportionately in the expensive school zone — 'basement homes are better homes in several ways at once.'
- The cycle-1 signature disease and exam 1's signature flaw; the fireplace's $52,343 raw 'premium' is the kill shot — it belongs almost entirely to the size and equipment of fireplace homes.
- Secondary: subgroup reversal (Simpson's) — a gap can shrink, vanish, or flip inside every subgroup.
- Cure: composition check first (how else do the groups differ?), then adjustment by regression.
managerial_phrasing: Before pricing the feature: the groups differ in [these other ways], so the raw gap bundles all of them — here's the gap after controls.
common_mistake: Saying 'the basement is worth $65K.' The honest naive sentence is: basement homes sell for $65K more — and they're different homes.

title: Disease: the truncated axis
body:
- A bar chart's y-axis starts above zero, visually inflating a small difference into a dramatic one; the numbers are honest, the geometry lies.
- Ratios of bar heights are the perceptual message — truncation breaks the ratio while leaving the labels technically true.
- Headline trap of Visualization. Cure: bars start at zero; if a zoomed view is genuinely needed, an axis break or an explicit callout says so.
managerial_phrasing: Does the picture's drama match the numbers' drama? Check where the axis starts before trusting a chart's story.
common_mistake: Defending the chart because the labels are correct. Charts persuade through geometry; correct labels on distorted geometry still deceive.

title: Simple regression: the trendline with receipts
body:
- price ~ sqft fits the line Excel's scatter trendline draws — now with readable output: slope $142.8/sqft, R² = .596.
- Predict by hand: 500 extra sqft ≈ $71K along the fitted line. The slope is dollars per one unit of x; multiply for your scenario.
- R² is the share of price variation the line accounts for — .60 means sqft alone tracks most of the story, not all of it.
- The fitted range matters: Eastville's largest home is 3,222 sqft; the line knows nothing about 5,000.
managerial_phrasing: Within the range we observed, each additional square foot associates with about $143 — explaining roughly 60% of price variation.
common_mistake: Treating the slope as a causal price and the line as valid beyond the data's edge.

title: Multiple regression: adjustment and the three fates
body:
- Adding controls (price ~ basement + sqft + age + beds + baths + school + style) asks: what's the basement gap among otherwise-similar homes? C(school) tells the model a column is categorical.
- The three fates — a naive number under honest controls can survive, shrink, or evaporate. Eastville: the $65K naive basement gap shrinks to a far smaller premium that survives; the $52K fireplace 'premium' vanishes (indistinguishable from zero); the sqft answer barely moves — some numbers are robust.
- No Excel twin exists for this. That absence is why the course exists.
managerial_phrasing: Controlling for what else the house is: the basement premium shrinks but survives; the fireplace premium was never real; square footage was honest all along.
common_mistake: Reading every coefficient shrinkage as 'the effect is fake.' The fates differ — the skill is saying which fate your number met.

title: Confidence intervals: the honest give-or-take
body:
- A coefficient is an estimate; the 95% CI is the range of values the data can't rule out. At n=108, those ranges are wide — visibly wide.
- The accountability lesson: a premium whose CI runs from near-zero to several times the point estimate cannot be quoted as a crisp number.
- Interval honesty is a memo requirement: every signed number carries its give-or-take, and 'give or take almost everything' is a finding.
managerial_phrasing: The best estimate is $X, give or take $Y — and if the low end changes the decision, the decision isn't settled.
common_mistake: Quoting the point estimate alone. The interval is not fine print; at this sample size it is most of the message.

title: 🔧 Recipe: the regression incantation
body:
- smf.ols('price ~ sqft + basement', data=df).fit() — formula on the left of ~ is the outcome, terms on the right are predictors, C(col) wraps categoricals.
- .summary() prints the table; you read coef, the 95% CI, and R². The rest of the printout is not course material.
- Recipe-tier: you will never derive this. Understand-tier is reading its output correctly — that part is examinable.
managerial_phrasing: The machinery is standard; the deliverable is the correct English reading of three numbers: the coefficient, its interval, and the fit.
common_mistake: Anxiety over the summary table's twenty statistics. Three are yours; the rest are someone else's exam.

title: Disease: correlation as causation
body:
- Association gets narrated as mechanism: 'sqft drives price,' 'engagement causes retention' — when the data shows co-movement only.
- Regression doesn't fix this; a coefficient is still an association, now with controls. Causal language requires design (experiments, natural variation), not just fit.
- Headline trap of the Correlation topic. Cure: write associations in association language; reserve 'drives/causes/adds' for claims your design can carry.
managerial_phrasing: Homes with more X sell for more — the data supports 'associated with,' not 'because of.'
common_mistake: Believing controls purchase causation. Adjustment removes named confounds; it cannot certify the mechanism.

title: Disease: extrapolation
body:
- The fitted line is quoted beyond the data's range: Eastville's model, fit on homes up to 3,222 sqft, asked to price a 5,000 sqft home.
- Outside the observed range the line is arithmetic without evidence — the relationship may bend, saturate, or break where you have no data.
- Secondary trap of the Correlation topic. Cure: state the fitted range with every prediction; refuse scenarios outside it or label them speculation.
managerial_phrasing: Our model has seen homes from A to B square feet; outside that range it's guessing in a straight line.
common_mistake: Trusting the formula because it computes. It always computes — the data's edge is where its authority ends.

title: Disease: coefficient misreading
body:
- The regression is right and the sentence about it is wrong: units mangled (per-sqft read as per-500-sqft), a categorical coefficient read against the wrong baseline, or certainty claimed that the CI doesn't support.
- The deep disease behind it: omitted variables — controls remove only what you named; the adjusted number still carries everything you didn't.
- Headline trap of Multiple regression; exam 1 realizes it as correct output under wrong narration. Cure: for every coefficient sentence — right units? right baseline? claim within the CI? what plausible confound is still missing?
managerial_phrasing: Each coefficient sentence gets checked three ways: the unit, the comparison baseline, and whether the interval actually licenses the claim.
common_mistake: Auditing the code and skipping the prose. In practice the model is usually fine — the sentence about it is where analyses lie.

title: The risk desk: dollarized error costs
body:
- Cycle 2's frame is the risk desk, not the loan office: the portfolio behind an MBS, where errors have prices from day one.
- A missed defaulter (false negative) carries the exposure — the average loan in our book runs ≈ $332K. A false alarm (false positive) costs an origination fee.
- The asymmetry is the whole game: with a ~25% default rate and that cost ratio, optimizing raw accuracy optimizes the wrong money.
managerial_phrasing: Our two mistakes have different prices — missing a defaulter costs orders of magnitude more than flagging a good loan — so we tune for the expensive one.
common_mistake: Evaluating a lending model like a trivia quiz. Symmetric scoring of asymmetric mistakes produces confident models that lose money.

title: Logistic regression: probabilities, not labels
body:
- Logistic regression outputs a default probability per loan (0 to 1), not a yes/no. The label comes later, when a threshold converts probability to decision.
- Separating score from decision is the point: the model estimates risk; the desk chooses what risk to tolerate.
- Fair-lending note: protected attributes (gender, age) are excluded from features on camera — an ECOA obligation, not a modeling preference.
managerial_phrasing: The model doesn't approve or reject — it prices risk. Where we draw the line is a business policy, made by us.
common_mistake: Reading model output as verdicts. The probability is the model's; the cutoff — and its consequences — are yours.

title: Train/test discipline
body:
- Split before anything else: fit on the training set, report performance only on the held-out test set. Test data must be untouched by every fitting decision.
- Training performance is a memory test; test performance is the forecast of behavior on loans you haven't seen — the only number the desk cares about.
- The discipline is procedural, not statistical: it fails through workflow leaks (peeking, reusing, shopping), not through math errors.
managerial_phrasing: Every performance number we quote comes from data the model never saw — otherwise it's a memorization score, not a forecast.
common_mistake: Reporting training accuracy as expected performance, or letting any modeling choice touch the test set before the final measurement.

title: Overfitting: memorization posing as skill
body:
- A model complex enough to memorize training data scores perfectly there and worse on new data. The tree makes it visible: unconstrained, train accuracy hits 1.000 while test lags far behind; capped at depth 3, the gap closes.
- The train-test gap is the diagnostic: large gap = memorization; small gap = learned structure.
- Complexity is a dial, not a virtue — depth is the one tuning knob in scope (max_depth).
managerial_phrasing: The model aced the homework it studied from; the test set tells us whether it learned anything transferable.
common_mistake: Chasing training performance. Perfect training scores are a warning sign, not an achievement.

title: The decision tree: stacked if-statements
body:
- A tree is s6's if, stacked: a flowchart of threshold questions ending in a default probability. Depth 3 reads on one slide.
- Its virtues are legibility (you can trace any loan's path) and honesty about overfitting (unconstrained depth memorizes visibly).
- Its cost: one tree is unstable — small data changes redraw the flowchart.
managerial_phrasing: The tree is a readable lending policy: you can follow any application down the branches and see exactly why it scored as it did.
common_mistake: Growing the tree deep 'for accuracy.' Depth buys memorization; the readable shallow tree is the honest one.

title: Random forest: a forest outvotes a tree
body:
- Many trees, each trained on a random slice of data and features, voting. The vote averages away single-tree instability — accuracy rises.
- The price is legibility: no flowchart exists; you get feature importances, not a path.
- This sets the course's standing question: the best model is the one you can't read — when do you accept that trade?
- Third of three in-scope models (logistic → tree → forest); switching models is one changed line, which is itself the lesson.
managerial_phrasing: The forest predicts better and explains less — whether that trade is acceptable depends on who must defend the decision.
common_mistake: Treating the forest's edge as free. The accuracy gain is real; so is losing the ability to trace why a loan was flagged.

title: 🔧 Recipe: the sklearn pattern
body:
- The unchanging four lines: train_test_split(...) → model = Constructor() → model.fit(X_train, y_train) → model.predict(X_test).
- Swapping models changes only the constructor line — LogisticRegression() to DecisionTreeClassifier() to RandomForestClassifier().
- Recipe-tier forever: internals are never course material. Understand-tier is the discipline around the recipe — what may touch the test set, and what the outputs mean.
managerial_phrasing: The machinery is four standard lines; our value-add is everything around them — the split discipline, the metric choice, the reading of results.
common_mistake: Studying fit()'s internals while misusing the test set. The recipe is safe; the workflow around it is where analyses die.

title: Comparing models: the s5 loop, full circle
body:
- for model in models: fit, evaluate, append a dict of results — pd.DataFrame at the end builds the comparison table. The construct you learned fetching API pages now benchmarks classifiers.
- Compare on identical splits and identical metrics, with the defaulter-recall column beside accuracy — accuracy alone ranks lending models wrongly.
- Model selection happens on training/validation evidence; the test set measures the chosen model once.
managerial_phrasing: One table, same data, same metrics, every candidate — and the ranking read on the metric that prices our expensive mistake.
common_mistake: Crowning the winner by test-set performance across many tries — that's shopping, and the winner's number is inflated by luck.

title: The confusion matrix, dollarized
body:
- Four cells: caught defaulters (TP) · missed defaulters (FN) · false alarms (FP) · correctly passed loans (TN). Every classifier metric is arithmetic on these four.
- The reveal: a high-accuracy model can hide a catastrophic FN count — accuracy near 87% while half the defaulters sail through.
- Dollarizing converts cells to money: FN × exposure vs FP × lost fee. The matrix becomes a P&L, and 'best model' becomes a finance question.
- Recall (share of defaulters caught) and precision (share of flags that were right) are the two readings that matter here.
managerial_phrasing: Here's the model's year in money: what the missed defaulters cost us versus what the false alarms cost us — that comparison picks the model.
common_mistake: Reporting accuracy and stopping. On imbalanced, asymmetric-cost data, accuracy is the one number guaranteed to mislead.

title: The threshold is a lending policy
body:
- Converting probability to decision requires a cutoff — and every cutoff is a different portfolio: lower it, catch more defaulters, refuse more good loans; raise it, the reverse.
- 0.5 is a default, not a decision. On imbalanced data it's usually the wrong one.
- The honest instrument is the sweep: recompute the dollarized confusion matrix across cutoffs and choose where the money says to stand. Model behavior can change qualitatively across the sweep — a failure visible at one cutoff can dissolve at another.
managerial_phrasing: We chose our cutoff by pricing the trade-off at each candidate level — the threshold is a business decision we can defend, not a software default.
common_mistake: Threshold naïveté: shipping 0.5 unexamined. The cutoff quietly encodes your cost judgment whether or not you made one.

title: Reading feature importances for business
body:
- The forest ranks which inputs its votes leaned on: in the loan book, leverage and capacity measures (LTV, DTI, property value, income) lead — a rankable sanity check against lending intuition.
- Importance is not effect size or direction: it says 'the model used this,' not 'this raises risk by X.'
- An unexplainable top feature is a finding, not a footnote — a dominant feature nobody can interpret (our credit-type quirk) belongs in the memo's limits section until it's understood.
managerial_phrasing: The model leans on the variables an underwriter would — with one exception we haven't explained, which we flag as an open item rather than hide.
common_mistake: Narrating importances as coefficients ('LTV adds X points of risk'). Importance ranks usage; it prices nothing.

title: Disease: leakage — the two-faced disease
body:
- The model sees information unavailable at decision time. Face one (framing, s15): the question itself smuggles the future — features described post-outcome. Face two (mechanical, s20): a column in the file encodes the outcome — our book's interest-rate field is blank for 99.5% of defaulters and 0% of payers; the missingness pattern is the label.
- Signature symptom: performance too good to be true — the '100% accurate' model. Removing the leak returns it to earth.
- Headline trap of Train/test and exam 2's signature flaw. Cure: for every feature ask 'would we know this at decision time?' — and treat implausibly good performance as an accusation, not a triumph.
managerial_phrasing: Every input passed the question: would the desk have this number on the day it decides? Anything downstream of the outcome is out.
common_mistake: Celebrating implausible accuracy. Near-perfect performance on a hard problem means the model found the answer key in the features.

title: Disease: test-set shopping
body:
- Many models or settings are compared on the test set and the best is reported as expected performance — the test set has become part of training, and the winner's score is inflated by selection luck.
- One honest use per test set: select on training evidence, measure the chosen model once.
- Headline trap of Model comparison. Cure: count how many times the test set was consulted; if more than once for the reported number, the number is shopped.
managerial_phrasing: This performance figure comes from a single, final measurement — not from picking the luckiest of many attempts.
common_mistake: Believing repeated test-set checks are diligence. Each peek converts the test set a little more into training data.

title: Disease: accuracy on imbalance
body:
- With a ~25% default rate, 'approve everyone' scores ~75% accuracy while catching zero defaulters — accuracy rewards siding with the majority class.
- The narration failure: accuracy headlined while the precision/recall lines sit printed and unread on the same page.
- Headline trap of Model evaluation. Cure: name the baseline (majority-class accuracy) first; report recall on the class that costs money; let the dollarized matrix arbitrate.
managerial_phrasing: Against a do-nothing baseline of 75%, what does the model add — and what share of actual defaulters does it catch?
common_mistake: Quoting accuracy without its baseline. On imbalanced data, a big accuracy number is the cheapest trick in the deck.

title: Disease: segment failure
body:
- Overall performance is fine; a by-segment breakdown shows the model failing exactly where it matters — weakest recall on the loan type that defaults most.
- Averages absolve: the aggregate metric launders a localized failure that a one-line groupby on the errors would expose.
- Secondary trap of Model evaluation (headline: accuracy on imbalance). Cure: break every headline metric by the business's own segments before signing; segment behavior can shift with the threshold, so check segments across the cutoff sweep, not at one cutoff.
managerial_phrasing: Overall the model performs at X — and here is the same metric for each segment, because a portfolio fails by segment, not on average.
common_mistake: Signing the aggregate. A model 'fine on average' can be systematically wrong for the riskiest slice of the book — the slice the desk exists for.

title: Prediction ≠ intervention
body:
- A default model predicts under the current process; it doesn't say what happens if you change the process. 'These loans would default' is not 'rejecting them saves their losses' — the counterfactual portfolio differs.
- Features predictive of default aren't levers: DTI predicts risk; forcing DTI down doesn't mechanically remove it.
- Secondary trap of Logistic regression (headline: threshold naïveté). Cure: memo language distinguishes forecasting under the status quo from claims about interventions.
managerial_phrasing: The model forecasts outcomes under today's process; what changes if we act differently is a separate question it wasn't built to answer.
common_mistake: Reading predictive features as control knobs. Prediction licenses triage, not causal claims about what changing a variable would do.

title: The answer memo: five sections
body:
- §1 The question, as framed at Ask · §2 The answers, with each number's history (what it was naively, what survived) · §3 The checks that make the numbers trustworthy · §4 The limits — what the analysis cannot support · §5 What's next.
- Fragments accumulate on the Answer Ledger all cycle; the final session is selection and compression, not drafting.
- The memo addresses a stated decision-maker in business English — zero code, zero jargon; every claim traceable to a check.
managerial_phrasing: One page: what you asked, what we found and how sure we are, how we verified it, what this doesn't tell you, and what we'd do next.
common_mistake: Drafting the memo at the end from memory. The ledger exists because memos assembled from accumulated, verified fragments beat memos written under deadline.

title: Interval honesty in the memo
body:
- Every signed number ships with its give-or-take, in dollars, in the sentence — not in a footnote.
- When the interval is wide enough to change the decision at one end, the memo says the decision isn't settled — that's a finding, not a failure.
- Prediction-scale version: performance quoted with its segment range, and the threshold's sensitivity stated.
managerial_phrasing: Best estimate $X, give or take $Y; if $X−$Y would change your decision, treat this as unresolved.
common_mistake: Rounding uncertainty away for a cleaner memo. The crisp version reads better and is the more dishonest document.

title: Disease: overclaiming
body:
- The memo asserts more than the analysis licenses: associations as causes, point estimates as certainties, one dataset's window as the world, predictions as intervention effects.
- The final disease because it's where all upstream sins get laundered into confident prose — examined structurally in every sign-the-number exercise.
- Headline trap of Answering. Cure: §4 (limits) is mandatory and specific; every claim gets the test 'which check backs this sentence?'; unbacked sentences get weakened or cut.
managerial_phrasing: Every sentence in this memo is either backed by a named check or explicitly labeled as judgment — and the limits section is real, not ritual.
common_mistake: Writing limits as boilerplate humility. Useful limits are specific enough to stop a particular misuse of your numbers.

title: The defense: attack bank and transfer rule
body:
- Final presentations run under the cold-call rule: any member, any question. The 15-question attack bank is the study guide — each question maps to a disease.
- The transfer rule: teams share the loan book but own their memos; defending means knowing your own numbers' history, not reciting generic answers.
- Dry runs at s24 are attacked by another team; what they expose becomes the s25 triage agenda. Being attacked early is the gift.
managerial_phrasing: Anyone on the team can trace any headline number back through its checks — that's the standard the defense tests.
common_mistake: Prepping by polishing slides. The defense grades the numbers' provenance; a beautiful deck with untraceable figures fails on the first question.

title: Out of scope: models we deliberately cut
body:
Cut and stays cut: boosting/XGBoost · SVM · neural networks · hyperparameter tuning beyond max_depth.
- Logistic, tree, and forest span the trade-offs that matter (legible vs accurate); further models add leaderboard points, not judgment.
- If an agent proposes XGBoost, that's normal — the verification skills transfer unchanged; the audit questions (leakage, shopping, segments, threshold) are model-agnostic.
managerial_phrasing: We audit any model with the same questions; the three we build are enough to learn every question.
common_mistake: Equating fancier models with better analysis. Every disease in the taxonomy afflicts XGBoost identically — judgment, not architecture, was the bottleneck.
